sec-1.title: Market size and growth
sec-1.draft:
Quick commerce grew fast in large Indian cities, with daily orders rising every quarter of the sample year [S1]. Most orders came from groceries and daily essentials delivered in under fifteen minutes [S1].

Analysts in the sample expect the market to keep growing, though more slowly than before, as platforms expand into smaller towns [S2]. Growth in smaller towns depends on enough order density to keep delivery costs low [S2].

sec-2.title: Key players and business models
sec-2.draft:
Three platforms, called Alpha, Beta and Gamma in this sample, handle most quick commerce orders [S3]. Alpha has the largest share of orders, followed by Beta [S3].

All three run dark stores: small warehouses close to customers that are not open to walk-in shoppers [S2]. A dark store keeps a few thousand fast-selling items, so a picker can pack an order in about two minutes [S2]. Placing dark stores within a short ride of most homes is what makes ten-minute delivery possible, and it is also the largest fixed cost of the model, because each store needs rent, staff and stock whether or not orders come in [S2, S3]. Platforms therefore open new stores only where they expect enough orders per day, and they close or merge stores that stay below that level for several months [S3]. In the sample, this careful expansion is described as the main reason the leading platforms have kept their losses from growing as fast as their order volumes [S3].

sec-3.title: Regulation and gig workers
sec-3.draft:
Delivery partners work as gig workers, so they are not employees of the platforms [S4]. A sample state law requires platforms to pay into a welfare fund for gig workers [S4].

The sample report found no national rule on delivery time targets.
